slides: Welcome back, and now the second kind of overlap question. Here the question gives us every fact we need. So we can find the exact number in each region.

slides.say: Let's go back to our fifteen students. Ten take art, and nine take drama. In the last lesson, both could be anything from four to nine.
at: Ten take art, and nine take drama

slides.say: Now we add one more fact. Exactly two students take neither art nor drama.
Let's hand out the places again. The ten shaded boxes are the art students, so five students don't take art.
at: Let's hand out the places again

slides.say: Exactly two of those five take neither. Let's mark them in grey.
So the other three students without art must take drama. Five minus two is three, and nobody else is outside art.
Drama has nine students, and three of them are drama only. So nine minus three, six drama places are left. They go to art students.
So exactly six students take both. Not a range this time, one number. The fact about neither fixed it.
at: So exactly six students take both

slides.say: With small numbers we can hand things out. With bigger numbers, there's a faster tool, the squares method.
We draw one long rectangle, and cut it into four boxes. Each box is one of the four regions. Neither, drama only, both, and art only.
It's the same as the two circles, just drawn in a line. Every student is in exactly one box. So all four boxes together are the total, fifteen.
The art bracket covers two boxes, both and art only. Together they're ten.
The drama bracket covers drama only and both. Together they're nine.
Careful here, this is a common mistake. The two brackets must share the middle box, both. If they don't share a box, there's no overlap at all.
Now we fill the boxes like a sudoku, starting from what we know. Neither is two.
Neither plus the whole drama bracket is two plus nine, eleven. That's every box except art only.
The four boxes make fifteen. So art only is fifteen minus eleven, four.
The art bracket is ten. Art only is four, so both is ten minus four, six.
And drama only is nine minus six, three.
Let's check. Two plus four plus six plus three is fifteen. It fits, and it's the same six as before.
We can start from any box the question gives us. Say the question gives art only instead. The same fifteen students, ten in art, nine in drama, and four take art only.
at: Say the question gives art only

slides.say: The art bracket is ten, and art only is four. So both is ten minus four, six.
The drama bracket is nine, so drama only is nine minus six, three.
Then four plus six plus three is thirteen students in at least one group. So neither is fifteen minus thirteen, two.
And we fill only the boxes we need. If they ask for both, we stop at both.

Sometimes neither isn't written as a number, but the words still tell us what it is. For example, each of thirty guests drank tea, coffee, or both. Eighteen drank tea, and seventeen drank coffee. How many drank both?
Every guest drank something. So nobody is outside both groups, and neither is zero.
Now it's an exact question, so let's draw the boxes. All four together are thirty. Tea is eighteen, and coffee is seventeen. And the first box, neither, is zero.
Neither plus coffee only is everyone outside tea. That's thirty minus eighteen, twelve. Neither is zero, so coffee only is twelve.
The coffee bracket is seventeen. So both is seventeen minus twelve, five.
The same happens with different things. Two friends have twenty different stamps together. One has twelve, and the other has eleven.

slides: Twenty counts only the stamps they have, so no stamp is outside both groups. Neither is zero.

slides.say: So we count each stamp once. Twelve plus eleven is twenty-three. But there are only twenty stamps, so twenty-three minus twenty, three stamps were counted twice. Both friends have those three.
Now compare it with a class of twenty students. Twelve play chess, and eleven play music.
Here some students may play nothing, so neither isn't given. Then it's a range again. Both is from three, the sum minus the total, to eleven, the smaller group.
So check what the total counts, not just one word. If it counts only people or things in at least one group, neither is zero. That's the box to start from.
at: If it counts only people or things

slides.say: There's one more region a question can ask about, exactly one. Exactly one means one group, but not both. So art only, or drama only.
In our boxes, that's four plus three, seven.
Without the boxes, add the two groups, then subtract both twice. Why twice? The six in both were counted in art and in drama. We don't want them in exactly one, so we remove both copies.
Ten plus nine is nineteen. Two times six is twelve. Nineteen minus twelve is seven. The same seven.
Let's sum up. In an exact question, we draw the four boxes. Neither, B only, both, and A only.
The two brackets share the middle box, and all four boxes make the total.

slides: And when everyone is in a group, neither is zero.

slides.say: We put in what we know, and fill the rest like a sudoku. Now let's practice it on three questions. I'll see you in the next video.
